The physician asks you to pull the complete electronic health records of 1,200 patients diagnosed with type 2 diabetes over the past two years, including full medical histories, lab results, imaging reports, medication lists, and personally identifiable information such as national ID numbers and contact details. The company wants the data uploaded to their secure cloud platform, but they have not provided any written data sharing agreement, nor have they obtained explicit patient consent as required under the PDPD and the hospital's internal confidentiality policies. They need the dataset within 48 hours to meet a grant submission deadline.
JOBFIT-HEALTH-MANAGEMENT-3.instructions: Explain how you would handle this request to ensure compliance with the PDPD and protect patient confidentiality.
choices: Refuse bulk identifiable EHR transfer without DSA and required consents under PDPL/hospital policy; offer lawful alternatives (ethics/IRB path, anonymized/minimized data, formal agreement) and do not upload to the company cloud in 48 hours under pressure.
Upload the full 1,200 identifiable records within 48 hours to meet the grant deadline.
Email national ID numbers and contacts to the physician’s personal Gmail for convenience.
Approve the transfer orally with no written agreement because the sponsor is a well-known pharma company.

JOBFIT-ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE-DATA-SCIE.scenario: A regional Saudi health authority has deployed a machine learning model to screen routine laboratory results for early signs of chronic kidney disease. In the target population, only about 2 % of individuals actually have CKD, resulting in a heavily imbalanced dataset. The current version of the model reports 96 % accuracy, yet clinicians have observed a high number of missed CKD cases that later required costly dialysis treatment. The medical director, focused on patient outcomes and resource allocation, has asked the data science team to evaluate the model more robustly and to recommend a metric that reflects the real‑world consequences of false negatives (undetected disease) versus false positives (unnecessary follow‑up tests).
JOBFIT-ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE-DATA-SCIE.instructions: Select and justify an appropriate metric for evaluating the CKD detection model that reflects the business cost of false negatives versus false positives, and convey your rationale in a clear, non‑technical summary for stakeholders.
choices: Reject accuracy as primary metric on 2% prevalence; recommend recall/sensitivity and/or cost-weighted false-negative focused metrics (e.g., F2, utility) and explain to the director that missed CKD (FN) is costlier than extra follow-up (FP).
Keep optimizing accuracy because 96% sounds strong to leadership.
Optimize only precision and ignore false negatives entirely.
Recommend random guessing as a fair baseline for clinicians.

JOBFIT-ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE-DATA-SCIE.scenario: You have been assigned to the predictive maintenance team at a major Saudi renewable energy firm that operates a fleet of wind turbines across the kingdom. Your colleague has built a classification model to predict turbine blade failure within the next month and reports a 100% recall on a validation set after using a feature that records the exact failure timestamp for each turbine in the past 12 months and also applying a normalization step to the entire dataset before the train-test split. Outline how you would scrutinize the validation results, pinpoint the data leakage, and redesign the data preparation and evaluation pipeline to enforce genuine train-test discipline and reliable cross-validation.
JOBFIT-ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE-DATA-SCIE.instructions: Explain how you would investigate the data leakage, correct the preprocessing, and perform proper validation to obtain realistic performance.
choices: Flag leakage: failure timestamp and fit-normalization on full data before split; remove post-failure features, fit preprocessors on train only, and re-validate with proper CV for realistic performance.
Accept 100% recall as proof the model is production-ready.
Add more leaked target-derived features to push accuracy higher.
Evaluate only on the same rows used for training to confirm stability.

JOBFIT-ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE-DATA-SCIE.scenario: A Saudi university consortium has developed an AI-driven scholarship eligibility model that combines GPA, standardized test scores, extracurricular participation, and a proxy for socioeconomic status derived from postcode. The model demonstrates 93% overall predictive accuracy, but a fairness audit reveals that female applicants from the Western provinces experience a false‑negative rate that is 2.5 times higher than male applicants from central provinces, resulting in significantly fewer scholarship offers despite similar academic profiles. The project team intends to roll out the system to all member universities in three months, arguing that the disparity is a minor artifact that can be addressed through post‑deployment monitoring.
JOBFIT-ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE-DATA-SCIE.instructions: Provide a comprehensive remediation plan for the fairness issue, including root‑cause analysis, corrective changes, re‑validation, and human oversight aligned with SDAIA AI Ethics 2.0 and Saudi PDPL.
choices: Pause deployment: analyze false-negative disparity drivers across demographic groups, re-balance training data representation, adjust group-specific decision thresholds, add human oversight, and document compliance with SDAIA AI Ethics guidelines.
Apply post-processing threshold adjustments to align overall demographic selection rates, while scheduling quarterly fairness reviews post-launch.
Retrain the eligibility model excluding geographical location proxies, validating secondary impact on overall 93% predictive accuracy.
Introduce a manual appeal workflow for rejected applicants while maintaining current model deployment timelines for member universities.
